source_document.body:
Start CDL Inc. is challenging its emergency removal from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration ’s training registry .
The Cinnaminson, New Jersey-based truck driving school said the FMCSA improperly used drivers’ later English-proficiency violations to justify shutting down its federally regulated training operations, according to a complaint filed Oct. 2.
But the 236-page complaint and exhibit packet presents questions beyond that legal dispute: A six-driver spreadsheet names another training provider, the attached roadside reports concern 10 different drivers, and a scanned removal notice makes substantive findings against a third school.
The school’s own account also contains unresolved date discrepancies, including an English-assessment certificate dated after the roadside inspection it allegedly preceded.
Start CDL filed the suit Oct. 2 in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against the U.S. Department of Transportation , FMCSA and Administrator Derek D. Barrs, seeking reinstatement and relief from the agency’s action.
FMCSA’s Aug. 31 notice immediately removed Start CDL from its training provider registry, along with more than 100 other schools.
The notice to shutdown arrived as federal regulators crack down on hundreds of commercial driver training providers and attempt to create stricter enforcement of CDL training .
The FMCSA notice prohibited Start CDL from conducting entry-level driver training, enrolling new trainees, certifying completion or uploading training certifications.
FMCSA cites safety risks
The agency said six trainees certified by Start CDL subsequently received English-language-proficiency violations during roadside inspections. FMCSA inferred that the drivers lacked the required proficiency when the school submitted their certifications, concluding that the provider had material deficiencies and demonstrated willful disregard of applicable requirements.
The notice invoked both an immediate public safety rationale and willful disregard as grounds for emergency removal.
English proficiency is a longstanding federal driver-qualification requirement. Enforcement guidance included in the exhibits describes restoration of out-of-service treatment for English-proficiency violations in June 2025.
Several attached inspection reports in the Oct. 2 complaint document specific communication problems or incorrect highway-sign responses. An Arkansas report describes difficulty answering questions about cargo, documents and air pressure. A Missouri report records four incorrect sign responses. Those accounts provide factual support for officers’ findings at the roadside.
They do not, by themselves, establish when the drivers completed training or their proficiency when certifications were uploaded — the connection at the center of the school’s challenge.
Driver records do not line up
The spreadsheet attached to the removal materials lists six drivers under Star CDL Training LLC. Its provider identifiers differ from Start CDL’s registry identifier.
None of those six names appears among the 10 unique drivers in the attached inspection reports. The report numbers also differ. Start CDL’s exhibits include training agreements connecting the school to three of the inspection subjects, but do not provide a reconciled six-driver roster with completion dates and certification upload records.
The notice describes the inspection reports as a representative sample, yet the packet does not explain how they correspond to the six drivers in the spreadsheet.
A scanned version of the notice also names Punjabi School of CDL Inc. in findings addressing deficiencies, immediate safety necessity and willful disregard. Another version is called Start CDL.
The discrepancies raise questions about how the FMCSA may have assembled and matched its evidence. The filing does not establish whether they reflect attachment errors, underlying data errors or another explanation.
School’s timeline also needs clarification
Start CDL argues in the complaint that later roadside violations do not establish deficient instruction or proficiency at the time of training. It also disputes FMCSA’s interpretation of a training provider’s responsibilities under federal entry-level driver training requirements.
However, the complaint and administrative petition describe cited inspections occurring between May and August 2026. The attached roadside reports instead span July 2025 through May 2026.
The complaint says driver Viacheslav Iroltuev passed the school’s English assessment with an 84% score in February 2026, before a May 13 roadside inspection. Both attached certificate copies show a date of July 2, 2026. The packet does not establish whether that is an issuance date documenting an earlier assessment.
School owner Vasyl Kushnir also says a July 23 DOT inspection prompted process corrections but identified no English-proficiency deficiencies. The exhibits contain no completed inspection report verifying that account.
Start CDL says it submitted an administrative-review petition and emergency-stay request Sept. 10. According to the complaint, those requests remained undecided when the lawsuit was filed Oct. 2.
The latest docket supplied for review lists no subsequent government response or judicial ruling. The administrative stay request included in the exhibits is directed to FMCSA; it is not a separately filed federal injunction motion.
FMCSA and Start CDL attorney Anton Kaminsky did not respond to requests for comment by publication time.
Why it matters: Removal prevents Start CDL school from providing federally required entry-level driver training, while the case raises questions about how FMCSA connects roadside safety violations to training providers.
